walkthroughs.body_html:
Theme E: Religion, Crime & Punishment — a core area of GCSE Religious Studies.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Theme E: Religion, Crime & Punishment brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Theme E: Religion, Crime & Punishment.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: When was UK capital punishment abolished?
How many aims of punishment are commonly listed?

options: Substance dualism means men and women are different.
Nirvana is the name of a Buddhist god.
Nirvana is the Buddhist version of heaven.
The 'blowing out' of the fires of craving, hatred and delusion — liberation from the cycle of rebirth (samsara), not a heavenly afterlife.

mcqs.q: What distinction matters for the free will defence to the problem of evil?
options: The free will defence solves all forms of evil at once.
Substance dualism means men and women are different.
Natural evil means evil that is good for nature.

Between moral evil (caused by free human choices) and natural evil (earthquakes, disease) — the free will defence directly addresses moral evil but struggles with natural evil, which isn't a product of free choice.

mcqs.q: What is substance dualism about mind and body?
options: Substance dualism means men and women are different.
The view (associated with Descartes) that mind and body are two distinct kinds of substance — a non-physical mind interacting with a physical body.
Nirvana is the name of a Buddhist god.
Substance dualism is the belief that humans have two personalities.
